title: Token-burn boundaries and hosting-fit intake - Sycamore Ventures
next_steps: Marcus to send pilot pricing spreadsheet and cost model
Schedule PoC scoping session with Priya and Sycamore's DevOps (Samir) next week
Customer to share latency targets and 2 sample workloads
Finance (Leah) to confirm budget band for Q1 pilot
action_items: Marcus Lee: Share detailed per-token/embedding pricing and expected unit cost ranges (due 2027-02-03)
Priya Nair: Prep benchmark script for 2 customer workloads and test plan (due 2027-02-05)
Samir Patel: Provide sample payload sizes and concurrency expectations (due 2027-02-02)
summary: Discovery with Sycamore Ventures focused on per-token economics, batching and KV caching levers, and which hosting mode (hosted vs dedicated vs private) fits their Q1 pilot budget and latency SLOs. Action items: pricing sheet, benchmark scripts, sample workloads. Security/residency and SSO/KMS concerns flagged for private deployment consideration.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-01-27 16:00 UTC | Duration 47m | Attendees: Marcus Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Elena Park (CTO), Jonas Meyer (Head of AI), Samir Patel (DevOps), Leah Ortiz (Finance)

[00:00] Marcus Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Marcus from Redwood Inference — I'm the AE on this account. Priya, our SE, is with me. How's everybody doing?
[00:08] Elena Park: Hey Marcus, good thanks. Busy week but excited to chat.
[00:12] Jonas Meyer: Hi all. Quick agenda from our side is: we want to understand unit costs per call, what levers we can pull to reduce spend, and whether we should start hosted or go straight to dedicated/private.
[00:25] Marcus Lee: Sounds good. We'll cover per-token pricing, batching/caching, and then talk about hosting modes and security. Priya will speak to benchmarks.
[00:34] Priya Nair: Hi team, quick note: we'll also want two representative workloads — one high-latency, few-shot chat flow and one short generation (200-400 tokens) for embeddings and rerank.
[00:44] Samir Patel: Yep we can share sample payloads. Our concurrency is spiky — typical burst to 120 reqs/sec for short gen, sustained 20-30 reqs/sec for chat during business hours.
[00:55] Leah Ortiz: And budget-wise we have roughly a $50k pilot budget for Q1 but need to see unit economics before committing more.
[01:05] Marcus Lee: Great, that's useful. On pricing: our hosted API pricing is per-token for generation and a separate per-embedding unit. For pilots we usually map expected token volumes to cost bands and show you batching/caching scenarios to illustrate best-case and baseline.
[01:22] Jonas Meyer: Can you give a concrete example? Say 300-token responses on average, 10k calls/day — what's the delta between naive per-token and optimized with batching/cache?
[01:32] Priya Nair: Sure — naive per-token might be X (we'll send exact numbers) but with continuous batching and prefix KV cache, you can cut per-token compute by 25-60% depending on hit rates. For short responses batching gives less benefit, but for chat flows with large KV cache reuse, the savings are big.
[01:50] Elena Park: You said KV cache — is that the same as Redwood's prefix cache? We call it context cache internally.
[01:56] Priya Nair: Yes, same idea. We cache the KV state for recurring prefixes or system prompts. In practice customers get ~40% effective token savings when their interactions reuse context.
[02:08] Jonas Meyer: Ok but what about latency tradeoffs when you batch? Our customer experience SLO is p95 < 350ms for the chat path.
[02:15] Marcus Lee: Good question. Batching trades latency for throughput. Our smart router can route latency-sensitive requests to lower-latency slots (dedicated or higher-tier hosted paths) while batching background jobs. So you can set policy: user-facing chat goes to low-latency pool, embeddings and bulk rerank go to batched pool.
[02:33] Samir Patel: If we wanted private deployment — air-gapped — how different are the unit economics? Any ballpark?
[02:40] Priya Nair: Private/on-prem usually shifts most cost to fixed infra (reserved GPUs, infra ops). Per-token compute costs can be lower if you fully utilize reserved capacity, but you take on ops and amortization. We'll model both: hosted (variable cost) vs dedicated (reserved capacity with monthly commit) vs private (capex + opcost).
[02:59] Leah Ortiz: For procurement I need transparent estimates: per-token at baseline, per-token with expected caching, and the monthly commit for dedicated.
[03:07] Marcus Lee: We'll prepare a spreadsheet with Monte Carlo scenarios: different hit rates for KV cache, batching levels, and concurrency shaping.
[03:16] Jonas Meyer: Do you support quantized model variants? We saw mention of 4-bit and 8-bit models — does that change accuracy?
[03:23] Priya Nair: Yes, we support quantized variants. Typically 8-bit has negligible quality delta for many tasks; 4-bit can be tricky for some open models. We'll run evaluation on your prompts as part of the PoC.
[03:35] Elena Park: Security checklist: SOC 2, SSO/SAML, audit logs, KMS integration. What do you have out of the box?
[03:43] Marcus Lee: Hosted is SOC2, SSO via SAML/OIDC, and you can configure KMS for key management on dedicated/private. Audit logs and request-level tracing are available in Redwood Console. We'll share the security pack.
[03:55] Samir Patel: If we do dedicated, is networking VPN/VPC peering supported? We need no public egress for traffic.
[04:01] Priya Nair: Yes, dedicated supports VPC peering and private connectivity. Private (on-prem) is fully air-gapped. There are slight differences in ops overhead.
[04:12] Marcus Lee: Back to unit economics — a few levers: batching window, concurrency shaping, prefix/KV cache hit rate, model size and quantization, and routing policies. Each has latency/cost implications.
[04:25] Jonas Meyer: Could you run a quick back-of-envelope? 10k calls/day of 300 tokens each, no caching, hosted.
[04:32] Marcus Lee: Off the cuff — we'll put exact numbers in the sheet — but naive hosted would be the per-token rate times total tokens. With batching and 30% KV cache hit, you could move to maybe 60-70% of naive spend.
[04:45] Jonas Meyer: And if we reserve dedicated capacity for a month, what does utilization need to be to be cheaper than hosted?
[04:51] Priya Nair: It depends on reserved commit and model. Typically you need 60-75% utilization of the reserved GPUs for dedicated to be cost-effective versus hosted variable pricing. We'll run your numbers.
[05:05] Elena Park: We're also concerned about burst capacity. We have marketing-driven spikes — can Redwood burst beyond reserved capacity?
[05:11] Marcus Lee: Yes — Dedicated can be configured with burst credits to use shared pool for short spikes. That is priced separately but gives you breathing room.
[05:20] Leah Ortiz: How do you handle billing for caching? Is it token-level after cache?
[05:25] Marcus Lee: Billing is on tokens processed by the runtime; effective tokens after cache reuse is what matters. So if KV cache reduces compute by cropping repeated tokens, your billed tokens drop accordingly. We'll show sample invoices in the pilot.
[05:38] Samir Patel: Any gotchas for embeddings? We store vectors and plan to rerank at query time. Will cache help?
[05:45] Priya Nair: Cache helps less for one-off embeddings. But for rerank and similarity where you call same candidates repeatedly, you can cache intermediate representations. Also caching of model outputs for identical queries helps.
[05:58] Jonas Meyer: Can Redwood do A/B between quantized and full-precision models? We want quality guardrails.
[06:04] Priya Nair: Absolutely — rollouts and canary deploys are part of Redwood Console. You can route a percentage to a quantized model and run evals on a holdout prompt set. We also have quality regression alerts.
[06:19] Elena Park: Good. Timeline: we want a pilot in February. Is that feasible?
[06:25] Marcus Lee: Yes — typical pilot 2-4 weeks. We'll scope a PoC: benchmarks, latency targets, cost model, and a go/no-go criteria.
[06:33] Samir Patel: For the PoC we need a test harness that we can run inside our network if we pick private. Do you provide one?
[06:39] Priya Nair: We provide a benchmark harness and can run it remotely or we can give you a containerized harness for on-prem runs.
[06:46] Jonah Meyer: (noise) Jonas: Sorry, typo.
[06:49] Marcus Lee: No worries. Question from Leah — what outcomes will convince you to go to dedicated?
[06:56] Leah Ortiz: If per-token cost after optimizations projects to < 40% of hosted naive baseline for our projected Q2 volume, and SLA meets our p95 latency target, finance will recommend dedicated.
[07:09] Priya Nair: Noted. We'll model that scenario.
[07:12] Elena Park: Any limitations around model types? We use some custom fine-tuned models and a few open LLM variants.
[07:18] Priya Nair: We onboard custom models — there's a short model vetting and optimization pass. For private/dedicated we can also load customer-provided artifacts; for hosted we typically bring in verified model containers. There may be a brief QA window.
[07:32] Jonas Meyer: Let's talk about instrumentation — per-route token-level breakdown and cold-start traces. Do you expose that?
[07:38] Marcus Lee: Yes, Redwood Console provides per-route cost and latency breakdowns, token-level accounting, and end-to-end traces. You can integrate traces into your observability stack.
[07:49] Samir Patel: On telemetry retention: how long do you keep request-level logs by default? We have compliance needs.
[07:55] Marcus Lee: Default retention is 90 days for hosted; for enterprise contracts we can extend retention or provide customer-managed log export to your S3 for archival.
[08:05] Leah Ortiz: For procurement we need SOC2 attestation plus a simple T&C addendum for data residency.
[08:11] Marcus Lee: We'll attach our SOC2 report and a data residency addendum template.
[08:18] Jonas Meyer: One practical thing — our prompt templates are 3-4 system messages long and often repeat. That suggests high KV reuse. Do you have heuristics to estimate hit rate?
[08:27] Priya Nair: Yes, we can profile your prompt set. Usually templates and system messages give ~50%+ reuse in chat-heavy flows. We'll run a small sampling analysis once you send representative logs.
[08:40] Elena Park: About the billing mechanics. If we route some requests to dedicated and some to hosted as overflow, how is that invoiced?
[08:46] Marcus Lee: You'll have a blended invoice: committed capacity charges for dedicated + usage-based charges for overflow hosted traffic. We'll break it down line-item so finance can reconcile.
[08:57] Samir Patel: For networking, if we do VPC peering, is there egress cost? We want to avoid unexpected network bills.
[09:03] Priya Nair: With VPC peering there can be cloud provider egress but we typically help configure private links to minimize cross-region egress. We'll map expected egress in the deployment plan.
[09:14] Jonas Meyer: Any limits on throughput per GPU? If we pick a big model, how many concurrent short queries can one GPU handle?
[09:21] Priya Nair: It varies by model and quantization. For small 20B-ish models with batching you can reach high qps; for 70B models lower per-GPU qps but larger context. We'll size GPUs in the pilot.
[09:33] Marcus Lee: Let's get concrete on next steps — Marcus will send the pricing sheet and a baseline vs optimized scenario. Priya will prepare the benchmark harness and test plan. Samir will send sample payloads and concurrency patterns. Leah will confirm budget band.
[09:46] Elena Park: Sounds good. Can we also get a sample invoice showing blended billing?
[09:51] Marcus Lee: Yes, we'll include a sample invoice and Monte Carlo scenarios.
[09:55] Jonas Meyer: Quick question — competitor comparison, you mentioned LLMCloud and FastServe. How does Redwood differentiate on cost tooling?
[10:02] Marcus Lee: Primary diff is production-first controls: finer routing policies, token-level cost attributions, and built-in batching/cache levers with console-driven recommendations (Redwood Optimize) so you can actually act on unit economics.
[10:16] Samir Patel: Will you run a short benchmark with our real prompts?
[10:20] Priya Nair: Yes — that's part of the PoC scope. We'll need 2-3 prompt sets and expected SLA targets.
[10:27] Leah Ortiz: We'll aim to share samples by Tuesday.
[10:31] Marcus Lee: Great. Any other blockers?
[10:34] Elena Park: Nothing immediate. We just want transparent modeling and a clear go/no-go after the 2-week pilot.
[10:41] Jonas Meyer: One last point — can you demo the console's per-route cost breakdown in the scoping call?
[10:46] Priya Nair: Absolutely, we'll include a short console walkthrough.
[10:50] Marcus Lee: OK wrapping up — recap: send pricing + Monte Carlo, bench harness + test plan, sample payloads, schedule PoC scoping. We'll target start week of Feb 8.
[11:04] Samir Patel: Works for us. Thanks.
[11:07] Leah Ortiz: Thank you both.
[11:09] Marcus Lee: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the spreadsheet.
[11:13] Elena Park: Bye.

(End of recording)
